name: software_architecture
description: Vetted gold-standard ontology slice for software architecture terminology. Built from canonical, peer-reviewed sources. Used as both (a) the gold-standard target for the pipeline test cycle and (b) the dataset materialized by the demo loader so users see exactly what the test sees.
license_note: Excerpts in paper_*.json files are paraphrased summaries of the canonical sources, structured for terminology density rather than reproduction. Each paper file carries a full citation pointing back to the original work.

taxonomies.title: Software Architecture
taxonomies.description: Top-level taxonomy covering architectural styles, distributed-systems primitives, and the trade-offs that shape system design.

concept_schemes.title: Architectural Styles
concept_schemes.description: Named, recurring shapes for organizing software components and their interactions. Each style imposes a coordinated set of constraints that yields specific runtime properties.

concept_schemes.title: Architectural Constraints
concept_schemes.description: Individual design constraints from which architectural styles are composed. The REST style, for example, is defined by its six constraints.

concept_schemes.title: Consistency Models
concept_schemes.description: Guarantees a distributed system makes about the ordering and visibility of updates across replicas.

concept_schemes.title: Consensus Protocols
concept_schemes.description: Algorithms by which a group of distributed processes agree on a single value, despite failures.

concept_schemes.title: Replication Strategies
concept_schemes.description: Approaches to keeping multiple copies of data in agreement, including conflict-free replicated data types.

concept_schemes.title: System Trade-offs
concept_schemes.description: Fundamental properties that a distributed system can offer, and the tensions between them (e.g., the CAP trio).

concept_schemes.title: Design Patterns
concept_schemes.description: Named, reusable solutions to recurring design problems. Includes both code-level patterns and architectural patterns such as CQRS and Event Sourcing.

concept_schemes.title: Domain-Driven Design Concepts
concept_schemes.description: Strategic and tactical concepts from Domain-Driven Design: bounded contexts, ubiquitous language, aggregates, context maps, and domain events.

concept_schemes.title: Enterprise Integration Patterns
concept_schemes.description: Messaging-oriented patterns for connecting distributed applications, as catalogued by Hohpe and Woolf.

concept_schemes.title: Quality Attributes
concept_schemes.description: Non-functional properties an architecture is expected to deliver: modifiability, performance, availability, scalability, security, testability. Used in trade-off analysis (e.g., ATAM).

class_hierarchy.title: Architectural Style
class_hierarchy.description: A named, coordinated set of architectural constraints that yields a specific set of runtime properties.

class_hierarchy.title: REST
class_hierarchy.description: Representational State Transfer: an architectural style for distributed hypermedia systems, defined by six constraints.

class_hierarchy.title: Client-Server Architecture
class_hierarchy.description: An architectural style separating user-interface concerns from data-storage concerns by partitioning components into clients and servers.

class_hierarchy.title: Layered Architecture
class_hierarchy.description: An architectural style in which components are organized into layers; each layer uses only the services of the layer immediately below it.

class_hierarchy.title: Microservices Architecture
class_hierarchy.description: An architectural style that structures an application as a suite of small, independently deployable services, each running in its own process and communicating via lightweight mechanisms.

class_hierarchy.title: Architectural Constraint
class_hierarchy.description: A design rule imposed on the elements and relationships of an architecture; styles are composed of constraints.

class_hierarchy.title: Client-Server Constraint
class_hierarchy.description: Separation of concerns between data storage (server) and user interface (client).

class_hierarchy.title: Stateless Constraint
class_hierarchy.description: Each request from client to server must contain all information necessary to understand it; the server retains no client context between requests.

class_hierarchy.title: Cacheable Constraint
class_hierarchy.description: Responses must be implicitly or explicitly marked as cacheable or non-cacheable, allowing clients and intermediaries to reuse them.

class_hierarchy.title: Uniform Interface Constraint
class_hierarchy.description: A small set of generic interaction primitives applied uniformly across components, decoupling implementations.

class_hierarchy.title: Layered System Constraint
class_hierarchy.description: Components see only the layer with which they directly interact; intermediaries can be inserted transparently.

class_hierarchy.title: Code-on-Demand Constraint
class_hierarchy.description: Client functionality may be extended at runtime by transferring executable code from the server. The only optional REST constraint.

class_hierarchy.title: Replicated Data Type
class_hierarchy.description: A data type whose instances are maintained as replicas across multiple nodes.

class_hierarchy.title: Conflict-free Replicated Data Type
class_hierarchy.description: A replicated data type whose replicas can be updated independently and concurrently without coordination, and which provably converge to a consistent state.

class_hierarchy.title: State-based CRDT
class_hierarchy.description: A CRDT where replicas exchange full state and merge by a commutative, associative, idempotent join function over a join-semilattice. Also called CvRDT.

class_hierarchy.title: Operation-based CRDT
class_hierarchy.description: A CRDT where replicas exchange operations, requiring the underlying delivery channel to provide exactly-once causal delivery. Also called CmRDT.

class_hierarchy.title: Consistency Model
class_hierarchy.description: A contract between a system and its clients about how concurrent reads and writes are ordered.

class_hierarchy.title: Strong Consistency
class_hierarchy.description: All clients observe the same most-recent successful write at any point in time.

class_hierarchy.title: Eventual Consistency
class_hierarchy.description: Replicas may diverge briefly but, given enough time without new updates, all replicas converge to the same state.

class_hierarchy.title: Causal Consistency
class_hierarchy.description: Operations that are causally related are observed in the same order by every process; concurrent operations may be observed in any order.

class_hierarchy.title: Linearizability
class_hierarchy.description: The strongest single-object consistency: every operation appears to take effect instantaneously at some point between its invocation and response.

class_hierarchy.title: Consensus Protocol
class_hierarchy.description: An algorithm by which a distributed set of processes agrees on a single value in the presence of failures.

class_hierarchy.title: Paxos
class_hierarchy.description: A family of consensus protocols for asynchronous, crash-failure systems, comprising proposer, acceptor, and learner roles.

class_hierarchy.title: Multi-Paxos
class_hierarchy.description: An extension of Paxos that amortizes the cost of leader election across a sequence of consensus instances.

class_hierarchy.title: Raft
class_hierarchy.description: A consensus protocol designed for understandability, decomposing consensus into leader election, log replication, and safety.

class_hierarchy.title: System Property
class_hierarchy.description: A guarantee a distributed system can choose to offer.

class_hierarchy.title: Consistency (CAP)
class_hierarchy.description: In CAP: every read receives the most recent write or an error. Equivalent to linearizability in the CAP formulation.

class_hierarchy.title: Availability (CAP)
class_hierarchy.description: In CAP: every request receives a non-error response, without guarantee that it contains the most recent write.

class_hierarchy.title: Partition Tolerance (CAP)
class_hierarchy.description: In CAP: the system continues to operate despite an arbitrary number of messages being dropped or delayed between nodes.

class_hierarchy.title: Hexagonal Architecture
class_hierarchy.description: Also called Ports and Adapters: the application core is shielded from external concerns by a ring of ports (interfaces it owns) and adapters that translate between ports and external technologies.

class_hierarchy.title: Event-Driven Architecture
class_hierarchy.description: An architectural style where components communicate by emitting and reacting to events; coupling is reduced because producers do not know consumers.

class_hierarchy.title: Design Pattern
class_hierarchy.description: A named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem in a context.

class_hierarchy.title: CQRS
class_hierarchy.description: Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separates the model used to update information (commands) from the model used to read it (queries).

class_hierarchy.title: Event Sourcing
class_hierarchy.description: Persisting the state of an entity as a sequence of immutable domain events rather than as the current state alone; current state is recovered by replaying events.

class_hierarchy.title: Strangler Fig
class_hierarchy.description: A migration pattern for incrementally replacing a legacy system by routing new functionality to a new implementation behind a façade, until the legacy code is fully strangled out.

class_hierarchy.title: Saga
class_hierarchy.description: A pattern for managing long-lived transactions across multiple services: each step has an explicit compensating action that undoes its effect if a later step fails.

class_hierarchy.title: DDD Concept
class_hierarchy.description: A concept from the Domain-Driven Design body of practice.

class_hierarchy.title: Bounded Context
class_hierarchy.description: An explicit linguistic and modelling boundary inside which a particular domain model applies; the same word may mean different things in different bounded contexts.

class_hierarchy.title: Ubiquitous Language
class_hierarchy.description: A shared vocabulary used identically by domain experts, designers, and code, scoped to a single bounded context.

class_hierarchy.title: Aggregate
class_hierarchy.description: A cluster of associated domain objects treated as a unit for the purpose of data changes, accessed only through a root entity.

class_hierarchy.title: Domain Event
class_hierarchy.description: Something of importance to the domain that has happened. Immutable, named in the past tense, and a primary building block of event-driven and event-sourced systems.

class_hierarchy.title: Context Map
class_hierarchy.description: A diagram or model showing all bounded contexts of a system and the integration relationships between them (shared kernel, customer-supplier, anti-corruption layer, conformist).

class_hierarchy.title: Integration Pattern
class_hierarchy.description: A reusable solution to a recurring problem in connecting distributed applications by exchanging messages.

class_hierarchy.title: Message Channel
class_hierarchy.description: A logical address through which one application sends messages and another receives them.

class_hierarchy.title: Message Router
class_hierarchy.description: A component that consumes a message from one channel and republishes it to a different channel based on rules over the message.

class_hierarchy.title: Message Translator
class_hierarchy.description: A component that transforms messages from one format to another between two applications that expect different schemas.

class_hierarchy.title: Publish-Subscribe Channel
class_hierarchy.description: A message channel that broadcasts each message to all interested subscribers.

class_hierarchy.title: Point-to-Point Channel
class_hierarchy.description: A message channel that ensures each message is delivered to exactly one receiver.

class_hierarchy.title: Request-Reply
class_hierarchy.description: A two-message conversation in which a requester sends a request and a replier returns a correlated response on a reply channel.

class_hierarchy.title: Quality Attribute
class_hierarchy.description: A measurable or testable property of a system that indicates how well the system satisfies its stakeholders' needs.

class_hierarchy.title: Modifiability
class_hierarchy.description: The cost and risk of making changes to the system.

class_hierarchy.title: Performance
class_hierarchy.description: Response time, throughput, and resource utilization under given workloads.

class_hierarchy.title: Availability (Quality Attribute)
class_hierarchy.description: The probability that the system is operational and able to respond when needed. Distinct from the CAP-A formulation: this measures continuous operability, not partition behaviour.

class_hierarchy.title: Scalability
class_hierarchy.description: The system's ability to handle increased load by adding resources.

class_hierarchy.title: Security
class_hierarchy.description: The system's ability to protect data and operations from unauthorized access while delivering authorized access.

class_hierarchy.title: Testability
class_hierarchy.description: The ease with which software can be made to demonstrate its faults.

class_hierarchy.title: Replication Topology
class_hierarchy.description: An organising structure for how writes are accepted and propagated among replicas.

class_hierarchy.title: Leader-Follower Replication
class_hierarchy.description: All writes go to a single leader; followers replicate the leader's change stream.

class_hierarchy.title: Multi-Leader Replication
class_hierarchy.description: Multiple nodes accept writes and propagate changes to each other; resolves write conflicts at merge time.

class_hierarchy.title: Leaderless Replication
class_hierarchy.description: Any node may accept a write; clients send writes to multiple replicas directly and use read repair and anti-entropy to reconcile.

property_definitions.title: satisfies constraint
property_definitions.description: An architectural style satisfies an architectural constraint.

property_definitions.title: composed of
property_definitions.description: An architectural style is composed of a set of constraints.

property_definitions.title: uses protocol
property_definitions.description: An architecture uses a consensus protocol.

property_definitions.title: trades off
property_definitions.description: A system property trades off against another system property under the CAP formulation.

property_definitions.title: converges via
property_definitions.description: A replicated data type converges via a specific mechanism (a join function or causal delivery).

property_definitions.title: service
property_definitions.description: A multi-sense term used across software-architecture literature. Tracked here as a property-definition with explicit senses to exercise the lexical-sense disambiguation pipeline.

property_definitions.title: clock
property_definitions.description: Multi-sense across distributed-systems literature: logical clocks (Lamport) versus physical (wall-clock) time.

property_definitions.title: implements pattern
property_definitions.description: An architectural style or system implements a design or integration pattern.

property_definitions.title: belongs to context
property_definitions.description: An aggregate, domain event, or model element belongs to a single bounded context.

property_definitions.title: affects quality
property_definitions.description: An architectural decision affects one or more quality attributes, positively or negatively.

property_definitions.title: routes via
property_definitions.description: A message flow routes via a specific integration pattern (channel, router, translator).

service.description: The term 'service' appears across multiple canon papers with distinct meanings. The pipeline must produce separate lexical_senses on the 'service' property-definition, not a single conflated sense.

consistency.description: 'Consistency' has two distinct technical senses: the C in CAP (linearizability) and the broader family of consistency models (eventual, causal, strong). The pipeline should subclass both under ConsistencyModel without conflating them.

replica.description: 'Replica' is used consistently across all canon papers that mention it. The pipeline should NOT split this into multiple senses — a regression toward over-splitting is detectable here.

availability.description: 'Availability' has two distinct senses in this corpus: CAP-A (formally defined as 'every request to a non-failed node receives a non-error response') and the SEI quality attribute (probability of being operational over time). The pipeline must produce distinct lexical senses or distinct classes for these — it must NOT conflate them into one.

pattern.description: 'Pattern' is used consistently as a named reusable solution across CQRS, Event Sourcing, Strangler Fig, and EIP. Single sense expected; over-splitting (one sense per source) is a regression.

context.description: 'Context' is multi-sense across the corpus: bounded context (DDD), execution context, application context. The DDD usage in paper_evans_ddd_bounded_context is sufficiently distinct that it should be modeled as its own class (BoundedContext), not as a sense of a generic 'context' term.

leader.description: 'Leader' has a single technical sense across consensus protocols and replication topologies: a node coordinating writes. Used in both Raft and leader-follower replication. Single sense.

clock.description: 'Clock' is multi-sense in distributed-systems literature: a logical clock measures causal precedence and has no relation to real time; a physical clock measures wall-clock time and is subject to drift and synchronization error. The pipeline must produce two distinct lexical_senses on the 'clock' property-definition.
